Build a small spreadsheet engine as a Python package `sheet` in this project (standard
library only, Python 3.10+), with tests in tests/. Work through it fully: it should all work when

API (`from sheet import Sheet, SheetError`):
- `Sheet()`; `sheet.set(ref, text)` sets a cell's text ('' clears it); `sheet.text(ref)` returns
  the raw text ('' when empty); `sheet.get(ref)` returns the computed value; `sheet.display(ref)`
  returns it as shown.
- References are a column of one or two letters and a row from 1 to 999, case-insensitive: A1,
  b7, AA10. A malformed reference passed to `set`, `text`, `get` or `display` raises
  `SheetError` with `.code == "#REF!"`.
- Cell text: empty is empty; text that parses as a number (like 12, -3.5, .5) is that number; text
  starting with `=` is a formula; anything else is a text value.
- Computed values: `None` for an empty cell, a float for numbers, a str for text, or a
  `SheetError` instance (an Exception with a `code` attribute) for an error. `get` returns the
  error instance; it does not raise.

Formulas:
- Numbers, cell references, ranges like A1:B3 (only as function arguments), parentheses.
- Operators, loosest to tightest: comparisons `= <> < > <= >=` (1 for true, 0 for false), then
  `+ -`, then `* /`, then unary minus/plus, then `^` (right-associative, binds tighter than unary
  minus: -2^2 is -4 and 2^3^2 is 512).
- An empty cell counts as 0 in arithmetic; a text cell in arithmetic is a `#VALUE!` error.
- Functions (case-insensitive): SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT over any mix of ranges and values
  (in ranges, only number cells count; text and empty cells are skipped; COUNT counts numbers);
  IF(condition, then, else) evaluates only the branch it takes; ABS(x); ROUND(x) and
  ROUND(x, digits), rounding halves away from zero.
- Errors: `#DIV/0!` (division by zero, AVG of no numbers), `#REF!` (bad reference),
  `#CYCLE!` (a cell that depends on itself, directly or not), `#NAME?` (unknown function),
  `#VALUE!` (text in arithmetic, a range outside a function, MIN/MAX of no numbers),
  `#ERROR!` (a formula that does not parse). An error in any input, including a cell in a range,
  makes the result that error.
- Values always reflect the current inputs: changing a cell changes everything that depends on it.

Display: empty is ''; errors show their code; text shows as is; a number with no fractional part
shows without a decimal point (3, -4, 0), others with up to 10 significant digits (2.5, 0.3333333333).

CSV:
- `Sheet.from_csv(text)`: the first row fills A1, B1, ...; the second row A2, B2, ...; empty
  fields stay empty.
- `sheet.to_csv(values=True)`: rows up to the last used row and columns up to the last used
  column, each cell as displayed (or as raw text with `values=False`), newline `\n`, standard CSV
  quoting. An empty sheet is ''.

Command line: `python -m sheet eval FILE.csv` prints `to_csv()` of the file;
`python -m sheet get FILE.csv REF` prints one cell as displayed. A file that cannot be read prints
an error to stderr and exits with status 1.

Done. Here's what the night city is made of:

**`src/scene.js` — `createScene(THREE)` → `{ scene, camera, update }`** (pure scene building, no renderer, no DOM — it uses `DataTexture` pixel buffers rather than canvas textures so it even runs headless):

- **Ground** (`src/scene.js:34`): a 504×504 plane with a procedural street texture — one tile per 12-unit grid cell paints a dark block interior, asphalt roadway with dashed centre lines, and kerb lines, so the ground itself shows the street grid.
- **Buildings** (`src/scene.js:159`): a 9×9 grid of cells (streets between them), two cells skipped for a plaza and a park → **79 buildings**, each an individual `Mesh` with `userData.kind = "building"` and the 12-unit cell pitch keeping every one inside its block. Heights come from a shuffled bag of **10 distinct values** (5–46 units, `src/scene.js:137`), so tall towers cluster toward the centre; each gets random rotation and slight jitter.
- **Lit windows** (`src/scene.js:66`): six façade material variants, each with a color map *and* an `emissiveMap` where ~42% of windows glow — mostly warm amber, some cool office blue, varied brightness; side-face UVs are scaled so window tiles stay a constant world size on every building regardless of height. Plus blinking red rooftop beacons on the tall towers and a small unlit moon disc in the sky.
- **Lights + fog** (`src/scene.js:226`): a hemisphere light (dim steel-blue sky over near-black ground), a **directional "moon" light** with shadows, and **6 warm `PointLight` street lamps** whose intensity flickers gently in `update()`. `scene.fog` (linear, near-black `#05070f`) fades the far edge of the city into the night; background color matches.
- **`update(seconds)`**: moves the camera in a slow orbit (~2.9°/sec, radius 74 ± 6, height 24 ± 6) with `lookAt(0, 10, 0)`, so it stays aimed at the city the whole time.

**`index.html`**: import map maps `"three"` → `./vendor/three/three.module.min.js`; full-window `WebGLRenderer` (ACES tone mapping, capped pixel ratio) with a `resize` listener, and a `setAnimationLoop` that feeds `clock.getElapsedTime()` into `update`. - Cell text: empty is empty; text that parses as a number (like 12, -3.5, .5) is that number; text

- Computed values: `None` for an empty cell, a float for numbers, a str for text, or a
  `SheetError` instance (an Exception with a `code` attribute) for an error. `get` returns the
  error instance; it does not raise.

Formulas:
- Numbers, cell references, ranges like A1:B3 (only as function arguments), parentheses.
- Operators, loosest to tightest: comparisons `= <> < > <= >=` (1 for true, 0 for false), then
  `+ -`, then `* /`, then unary minus/plus, then `^` (right-associative, binds tighter than unary

## Package `sheet/` (stdlib only, 3.10+)

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `sheet/__init__.py` | Public API: `from sheet import Sheet, SheetError` |
| `sheet/refs.py` | Reference parsing/validation: `A1`, `b7`, `AA10` → `(column, row)`; 1–2 letters, rows 1–999, case-insensitive |
| `sheet/errors.py` | `SheetError(Exception)` with `.code`, plus the six code constants |
| `sheet/formula.py` | Tokenizer, recursive-descent parser and evaluator for `=` formulas |
| `sheet/engine.py` | `Sheet`: storage, cell classification, lazy evaluation, cache invalidation, `text/get/set/display` |
| `sheet/csvio.py` | CSV parsing/rendering via `csv` module |
| `sheet/__main__.py` | `python -m sheet eval FILE.csv` / `get FILE.csv REF` |

**Cell classification** (`engine.py:36-49`): `''` → `None`, numeric text (regex, so `12`, `-3.5`, `.5`, `1e5` work but `1_0`/`nan` stay text) → float, leading `=` → formula, otherwise text.

**Formulas**: precedence runs comparisons (`= <> < > <= >=`, result 1/0) → `+ -` → `* /` → unary → `^`, right-associative and tighter than unary minus, so `-2^2` = −4 and `2^3^2` = 512. Ranges (`A1:B3`) are accepted only as direct arguments of SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX/COUNT — a bare `=A1:A3` is `#VALUE!`. SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX/COUNT skip empty and text cells in ranges and propagate any error cell they cover; IF evaluates only the branch it takes (an error in the untaken branch is never seen); ROUND uses `Decimal` with `ROUND_HALF_UP` so halves go away from zero. Empty cells coerce to 0 in arithmetic; text in arithmetic is `#VALUE!`. `#CYCLE!` comes from marking dependencies during evaluation — the engine detects a self-reference in the current evaluation chain and propagates the cycle to every cell downstream of it.

**Freshness**: `set()` clears the whole memo and rebuilds dependency info, and each formula evaluation re-reads current cell values, so no value is ever stale; `get()` returns error instances rather than raising, and only malformed references raise `SheetError` with `.code == "#REF!"`.

**Display** (`engine.py`): `''` for empty, the code for errors, text as-is, integral numbers without a decimal point (3, −4, 0), everything else via `%.10g` → `2.5`, `0.3333333333`, `1.414213562`.

**CSV**: `from_csv` fills A1, B1, … per row and leaves empty fields as empty cells; `to_csv` covers up to the last used row/column, padding ragged rows, `\n` line endings, standard quoting, and `''` for an empty sheet; `values=False` emits raw cell text. `eval` writes `to_csv()` verbatim so the output ends in exactly one newline.

## Tests `tests/` (5 files, 148 tests)

`test_sheet.py` (API, refs, classification, display), `test_formulas.py` (precedence, associativity, comparisons, every error code), `test_functions.py` (ranges, laziness, COUNT/AVG/MIN/MAX edge cases), `test_csv.py` (round trips, quoting, bounds), `test_cli.py` (in-process `main()` plus real `python -m sheet` subprocesses, including a chmod-000 file and a directory to prove the exit-1 path).

→ Ran 148 tests in 0.15s — OK

Build a night city scene with three.js in this project. three.js is already here at
vendor/three/three.module.min.js (import it as "three" through an import map; there is no network,
so use only files in this project).

1. `src/scene.js` exports `createScene(THREE)` returning `{ scene, camera, update }`:
   - a ground plane and at least 40 buildings of varied heights (at least 8 different heights)
     laid out on a street grid; give every building mesh `userData.kind = "building"`
     (an InstancedMesh with that tag counts each instance);
   - lit windows: building materials (or separate window meshes) with an emissive color or an
     emissive map, so some windows glow;
   - at least two lights, one of them a directional, point or spot light (the moon or street
     lights), and fog;
   - `update(seconds)` moves the camera slowly around the city (it must move between t=0 and t=5)
     and keeps it looking at the city.
   `createScene` must not create a renderer or touch the DOM: it only builds the scene.
2. `index.html` shows the scene full-window: a WebGLRenderer, resizing with the window, and an
   animation loop that calls `update`. It must load and run without errors in the browser.

The scene should read as night: mostly dark, with glowing windows. Check your work as far as you
can, then tell me what you built.
turns.answer:
Everything re-checks out against the current files, so here's what's in the project now.

## What I built

**`src/scene.js`** (578 lines) — `createScene(THREE)` returns `{ scene, camera, update }` and nothing else. It creates no renderer and touches no DOM: every texture is generated in memory as a `DataTexture`, so the module also runs headless under plain Node.

- **Layout**: a 9×9 street grid of blocks (`BLOCK_SPACING = 30`, so ~270 units across), with the middle row and column left open as two main avenues. 68 individual building meshes plus an `InstancedMesh` outer ring of distant towers — **123 buildings tagged `userData.kind = "building"`** (the instanced mesh is tagged too and carries a `heights` array). Heights run 9→96 with **62 distinct values**, biased taller toward downtown, plus a few vacant lots, setback rooftop annexes, and red blinking beacons on the tallest towers.
- **Lit windows**: each facade gets a `MeshStandardMaterial` built from one of 18 procedural window textures used as both `map` and `emissiveMap`, with a warm emissive colour and randomized `emissiveIntensity` — some buildings are dimmed as "dark towers", so lit windows are patchy rather than uniform.
- **Light and fog**: 7 lights — a low `HemisphereLight` (deep-blue sky over near-black ground), a cool `DirectionalLight` moon, and 5 warm `PointLight`s down the avenues — plus `FogExp2(0x060a15, 0.0024)` so the far skyline dissolves into haze. A billboarded moon with a soft halo and 1400 `Points` stars are deliberately `fog: false`.
- **Life**: 22 instanced cars with glowing tail/head emissive run along the avenues, street lamp heads and their additive glow pools breathe, and the moonlight intensity drifts.
- **`update(seconds)`**: the camera orbits slowly (angle `t * 0.055`, radius 300 ± 48, altitude 78 ± 26) and calls `lookAt` on a target that wanders a couple of dozen units around downtown, so the city stays framed while the view slides.

**`index.html`** — import map maps `"three"` → `./vendor/three/three.module.min.js`; full-window `WebGLRenderer` (antialias, DPR capped at 2, ACESFilmic tone mapping), a `resize` handler that updates `camera.aspect` + projection matrix + renderer size, and a `setAnimationLoop` that feeds `clock.getElapsedTime()` into `update` before rendering. A tiny caption overlay reports the error text and stops the loop if anything throws, instead of leaving a silently black canvas.

## How I checked it

Headless, against the vendored r182 build under Node: 123 tagged buildings / 62 distinct heights, 68 building meshes all carrying an emissive window map, lights `[Hemisphere, Directional, 5×Point]`, `FogExp2`, camera at `(300, 78, 0)` at t=0 vs `(297.9, 82.1, 84.1)` at t=5 — **84.18 units of travel**, so it definitely moves between those two times. A ray check over t=0→120 found the worst perpendicular miss of the city centre is **28 units** against a ~135-unit city half-extent, i.e. the frame stays over the city the whole way around. `grep` for `document` / `window` / `WebGLRenderer` / `canvas` / `renderer` in `src/scene.js` returns nothing.

Then for real in a browser: I served the folder over `http://127.0.0.1:8931` (ES modules need a server, `file://` would block the import) and drove headless Chrome over CDP. **Zero page errors and zero console exceptions**, one canvas attached, renderer info live at 424 draw calls / 7,908 triangles / 38 textures / 8 programs, `contextLost: false`, and the camera advanced 59.2 units between frame 5 and frame 55 — so the animation loop really is running and `update` really is moving it. Two screenshots decoded with a small pure-Python PNG reader came back at mean luminance ~10/255 with ~95% of pixels below 20 and only ~0.9% above 120: a dark frame with scattered bright specks, which is the night-with-glowing-windows reading you asked for.

Two things worth flagging from that process. First, a real false alarm: my earlier browser run failed with `createScene` undefined, and it turned out **another project's server had grabbed port 8123** and was serving a different app's `index.html` — nothing was wrong with this code; re-running on a fresh port passed. The check now prints the page title and module state up front so a mix-up like that can't masquerade as a bug. Second, a limitation: the headless browser used a software GL path, so the draw-call/triangle counts tell you it renders, not how fast it'll be on your GPU, and my visual confirmation is pixel statistics plus ASCII previews rather than eyes on the image. Worth a look in a normal browser to judge the mood — if the windows are too sparse or the fog too thick, `emissiveIntensity` and the `FogExp2` density are the two knobs to turn.

I deleted the temporary verification scripts and stopped the test server; the tree is just `index.html`, `src/scene.js` and `vendor/`. To view it: `python3 -m http.server 8931` in the project folder and open `http://127.0.0.1:8931/index.html`.
